131.quote_or_event: In 1675 the ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi by the Mughal authorities. He is remembered as the second Sikh martyr and for his stand for religious freedom; Sikh tradition holds that he accepted death rather than yield.
131.explanation: Sikh memory treats Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom as the model of a principle held more dearly than one's own life.
131.tie_back: The Kural ranks right conduct above life itself; the Guru's martyrdom is Sikhism's defining example of exactly that ranking.
131.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Tegh Bahadur' (Tamanna Nangia, fact-checked by Britannica Editors)
131._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on conduct above survival, but the martyrdom concerns religious freedom rather than personal decorum as such, and details beyond the Britannica summary are left out.

132.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, as many as are the sins one commits, so many are the chains around his neck. If he possesses virtues, then the chains are cut away; these virtues are his brothers, his true brothers.”
132.explanation: Guru Nanak says faults bind a person like chains, while virtues free him and stand by him like real kin.
132.tie_back: The Kural finds conduct to be the one true companion after weighing every alternative; Guru Nanak calls virtues a person's only true brothers.
132.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
132._accuracy_note: Strong fit on virtue as the one dependable companion; the Kural's stress on guarding conduct even through hardship is not stated.

133.quote_or_event: “God does not ask about social class or birth; you must find your true home. That is your social class and that is your status - the karma of what you have done.”
133.explanation: Guru Nanak rejects birth as the measure of a person and says one's real class and standing are the deeds one has done.
133.tie_back: The Kural says right conduct is itself noble birth and a lapse makes one's birth low; Guru Nanak likewise makes deeds, not lineage, one's true jaat and pat.
133.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1330, Raag Prabhati, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
133._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one with the universalist reading of the couplet; it fits less well with Parimelazhagar's station-based reading, which Sikh teaching rejects.

134.quote_or_event: “He alone is a Brahmin, who knows God. He chants and meditates, and practices austerity and good deeds. He keeps to the Dharma, with faith, humility and contentment.”
134.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines the Brahmin by inner knowledge and conduct, not by descent or ritual learning.
134.tie_back: The Kural says a Brahmin's conduct, not his Vedic recitation, is what keeps his birth from ruin; Guru Nanak goes further and makes conduct the whole of what a Brahmin is.
134.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
134._accuracy_note: Strong fit on conduct over learning; but where the Kural still assumes a hereditary Brahmin, Sikh teaching rejects caste by birth altogether.

135.quote_or_event: “One whose heart is filled with jealousy of others, never comes to any good.”
135.explanation: Guru Ram Das warns that a person who harbours envy of others will never prosper.
135.tie_back: The Kural builds on the proverb that envy and prosperity never meet; Gurbani states that same incompatibility outright.
135.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 308, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
135._accuracy_note: Matches the analogy half of the couplet closely, but says nothing about conduct being the condition of eminence.

136.quote_or_event: “Those who remain awake and aware are saved, while those who sleep are plundered.”
136.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that only constant alertness against the vices keeps one's inner wealth from being stolen.
136.tie_back: The Kural's strong-minded never slacken because they know the harm a lapse brings; Gurbani likewise prizes unbroken vigilance and warns that the careless are robbed.
136.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 34, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
136._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on steady vigilance and its stakes; the Gurbani context is spiritual wakefulness in Naam rather than social conduct.

137.quote_or_event: “As are the deeds done, so is the reputation one acquires.”
137.explanation: Guru Nanak says the name a person earns follows directly from the deeds he does.
137.tie_back: The Kural says conduct brings eminence and a lapse brings blame; Guru Nanak ties reputation to deeds in the same direct way.
137.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
137._accuracy_note: Strong fit on deeds determining honour or dishonour; the Kural's paradox of blame 'one need never have suffered' is absent. The same salok supplies Kural 140.

138.quote_or_event: “As she has planted, so does she harvest; such is the field of karma.”
138.explanation: In his Baarah Maahaa, Guru Arjan calls the body a field of deeds in which each person reaps what she has sown.
138.tie_back: The Kural calls good conduct a seed and bad conduct a lasting source of sorrow; Gurbani uses the same sowing-and-reaping image for deeds.
138.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 134, Raag Maajh, Baarah Maahaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
138._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the seed-and-harvest image of conduct; the Sikh frame adds that grace and Naam finally outweigh karma, which the couplet does not.

139.quote_or_event: “So speak the Truth, in righteousness, and do not speak falsehood.”
139.explanation: Sheikh Farid's hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib tells the seeker to speak only truth and righteousness.
139.tie_back: The Kural says the disciplined cannot utter evil words even by a slip; Farid gives the positive rule of speech such people live by.
139.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Asa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
139._accuracy_note: Next-best: a command about truthful speech, not the Kural's point that habituated conduct makes evil speech impossible even in an unguarded moment.

140.quote_or_event: “If an educated person is a sinner, then the illiterate holy man is not to be punished.”
140.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that learning counts for nothing at the reckoning; a learned wrongdoer is judged by his deeds, while an unlettered good person is safe.
140.tie_back: The Kural says the much-read who do not live well with the world remain ignorant; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to let book-learning stand in for right living.
140.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
140._accuracy_note: Strong fit on conduct over learning; the Kural's specific test of 'harmony with the world' is broader and more social than the salok.
